title: Archaeologists May Have Found the World's Oldest Shipwreck
summary:
Archaeologists may have found the world's oldest shipwreck, or at least, a strong candidate for the title. Based on clues from its cargo, including pottery vessels, a research team has tentatively dated the wreck to around 2700-2400 BCE, but much work remains and a paper is yet to be published in a peer-reviewed journal.

Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, Antalya, found the wreck in shallow waters off Kekova, west of Antalya in Turkey, in 2024, acting on clues from local seafarers. Earlier this year, he asked a colleague to help date some of the pottery vessels found on the wreck.

There is now nothing to see of the ship itself, owing to underwater exposure. What remains is its cargo, embedded in the rocky slope along the Kekova coast, and the ship now rests on the seabed between two islands. The team believes it likely sought refuge in calmer lee waters during a storm while traveling along the coast of southern Turkey.

Divers worked over the past four months to extract pottery from barnacles clinging to the rocky underwater slope. The cargo included large ceramic storage vessels, or amphorae, which once contained products from regions of the eastern Mediterranean.

The pots were large, egg-shaped, flat-based jars with two handles, many with a raised horizontal clay belt around the widest part. Their shape and manufacturing technique help researchers date the cargo, and by extension the ship itself, though the precise dating is still under consideration, and earlier or later dates are also possible.

If the dating holds, the discovery could transform understanding of ancient Mediterranean connections during the Early Bronze Age, around 4,500 years ago.
why_it_matters: If the dating holds, this wreck could rewrite what we know about how far ancient Mediterranean peoples travelled and traded around 4,500 years ago.

background_read: Archaeologists study things people left behind long ago, and objects found underwater can survive for a very long time.
Pottery is especially useful because its shape and the way it was made change over time, so experts can use it to judge how old a find is.
In the ancient Mediterranean, ships carried goods such as pottery between coastal places, and a wreck can show which places were connected by trade.
When only the cargo survives, researchers must piece together the story from what remains on the seabed.
